title: nvlink-and-pcie-saturation-impact-on-kv-spillback-trace-notes
content:
Context:
This is a working log of the NVLink vs PCIe cross-GPU effects observed during KV cache spillback/paging experiments. Goal is to understand how interconnect saturation changes eviction behavior, reuse-rate profiles, and tail latency under multi-tenant synthetic workloads. Not a final writeup — notes, trace excerpts, and hypotheses for follow-up experiments.

Motivation / hypothesis:
- We suspect that when model shards or KV pages are pulled across NVLink vs PCIe (depending on instance type / topology), the increased transfer latency and reduced effective bandwidth causes the eviction / re-request cycle to amplify, increasing cold-miss tail latency and eviction churn.
- Secondary hypothesis: small frequent cross-GPU reads (hot microbursts) hit PCIe lanes more than NVLink in our hybrid rack, causing queueing at the host DMA channels and producing asymmetric degradation compared to single-GPU workloads.

Testbed and configuration (quick summary):
- Hardware: 2x NVIDIA A100-80GB per server (NVLink enabled between the two GPUs), nodes connected with PCIe Gen4 to host. Also ran tests on older p4d-style instances (no NVLink between GPUs; inter-GPU via PCIe/host).
- Runtime: serving-runtime commit 4f9a3c2 (wip: spillback-throttle flags) + instrumentation branch (tracebench patches).
- KV config: 64KB page size, adaptive-ttl disabled, spillback-to-remote-gpu enabled, local-residency-target=0.75, eviction-max-burst=3.
- Workload: multi-tenant mix of long-context chat traces (avg seqlen=1024) plus many short queries (avg seqlen=64) at 1200 qps aggregate. Synthetic trace generator used to create hot keys plus long-tail keys with Zipf alpha=1.1.
- Observability hooks: per-GPU DMA counters, nvlink-utilization (from nvidia-smi nvlink stats), host PCIe read BW (perf counters), runtime eviction logs (sample rate 1/1000), and per-request KV page fetch traces (correlate request_id -> page_id -> src_gpu).

Key observations:
1) NVLink-enabled node behavior:
   - NVLink utilization peaks at ~70–80% during sustained 800 qps of long-context workload; tail latency remains stable (p95 ~ 38ms seq token generation).
   - KV page fetch latency across NVLink median ~ 280us, p99 ~ 1.4ms. Eviction churn moderate: eviction rate ~ 0.8 pages/sec per GPU; reuse-after-evict rate low (~0.02).

2) PCIe-only (no NVLink between GPUs) behavior:
   - Host PCIe read BW reported by perf counters saturates intermittently with bursts correlated to short-query microbursts. Measured sustained bursts up to 9 GB/s on the host channel (per direction) causing queueing at the host DMA submission path.
   - Cross-GPU page fetch median ~ 640us, p99 ~ 6.8ms (significantly higher than NVLink).
   - Eviction churn increases sharply: eviction rate ~ 3.4 pages/sec per GPU, reuse-after-evict higher (~0.12) but many of those are immediate re-requests causing additional paging.
   - Observed increase in tail token-generation latencies: p95 jumped to ~220ms, p99 > 1.6s in hotspots.

3) Microburst patterns matter:
   - When short queries are batched tightly (bursts of 50 qps for 200ms windows), PCIe host queues back up quickly; NVLink shows better smoothing due to its lower per-transfer overhead and peer-to-peer DMA semantics.
   - Our runtime’s default spillback policy currently does not account for interconnect type; it simply prefers remote-GPU spillback when local residency pressure exceeds threshold.

Representative trace excerpts (sanitized):
- Request 0x7f9a..: NEED_PAGE page_3 from gpu0 -> gpu1 (PCIe): fetch_start=2025-02-25T15:42:11.321Z fetch_end=2025-02-25T15:42:11.962Z fetch_ms=641.0 evict_candidate=page_17 evict_time=2025-02-25T15:42:11.966Z
- Request 0x8c2b..: NEED_PAGE page_3 from gpu0 -> gpu1 (NVLink): fetch_start=2025-02-24T13:12:05.914Z fetch_end=2025-02-24T13:12:06.194Z fetch_ms=280.0 evict_candidate=page_47

Bandwidth correlation (high level):
- NVLink runs: higher raw BW but more uniform; fewer queueing spikes.
- PCIe hosts: larger variance; root cause seems to be host-side DMA submission concurrency limits and PCIe fabric contention with NIC (RDMA) traffic in some tests.

Eviction dynamics insight:
- On PCIe-only nodes, the runtime sometimes evicts pages that are about to be reused because remote fetch latency is non-negligible; the eviction decision uses a residency scoring heuristic that currently weights recency more than cross-node fetch cost.
- Result: churn loop where page evicted -> immediate re-request -> long fetch -> increased latency -> pressure -> more evictions. This is visible in trace clusters where same page_id appears in eviction and fetch logs within < 2s windows.

Small experiment: throttling cross-node fetches
- Enabled spillback-throttle config: max-concurrent-remote-fetches=12, per-src-gpu-window=100ms.
- Effect on PCIe nodes: p95 token latency cut from 220ms -> 120ms; eviction rate dropped ~30%; overall throughput slightly reduced (~5%) but tail improved.
- However, this caused some tenants with hot keys that were not colocated to see increased error rates (time-outs) if quota of remote fetches exhausted.

Operational recommendations (initial):
1) Runtime should be topology-aware: detect NVLink adjacency vs PCIe-only and bias spillback toward NVLink peers first when remote residency is considered cheaper than remote host+PCIe.
2) Adjust residency scoring: include estimated cross-node fetch cost (based on measured median fetch_ms per path) into eviction scoring so we avoid evicting pages that would be expensive to rehydrate.
3) Introduce microburst smoothing for PCIe nodes: dynamic windowing that stalls or queues short-query bursts to avoid DMA queue saturation (or coalesce fetches).
4) Default conservative throttle for remote fetches on PCIe-only nodes with clear admin override for dedicated latency-sensitive tenants.
5) Add an operator dashboard showing interconnect type, per-path median fetch latency, and a hot-referenced-pages heatmap so SEs can quickly understand cross-GPU penalties.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quantify interaction with NIC traffic: do we see worse results when network RDMA flows are active? Add NIC tx/rx baseline experiments and isolate PCIe lanes.
- How do different page sizes (32KB vs 64KB vs 128KB) change transfer overhead and burstiness across PCIe? Larger pages reduce per-transfer overhead but increase chance of unnecessary data movement.
- Can we batch remote page fetches strictly within request-local windows (coalescing fetches that share page prefixes) to reduce PCIe pressure?
- Should we prefer spilling back to NVMe (host SSD) instead of remote GPU when cross-node costs exceed threshold? Need cost-latency tradeoff curves.

Next steps / experiments planned:
- Run a controlled matrix: [NVLink vs PCIe] x [page sizes 32/64/128KB] x [burst pattern short/long] x [network background RDMA on/off]. Measure: eviction rate, reuse-after-evict, per-path fetch med/p99, p95/p99 token latencies.
- Prototype scoring change: add remote_fetch_cost_estimate as additive penalty in eviction score; run AB test on staging cluster.
- Implement improved telemetry: log per-page last-remote-fetch-latency, and surfacing per-path medians in tracebench output (PR in flight: see linked PR).

Notes to self / admin:
- See JIRA-REINF-3832 for experiment tracker.
- Refer to PR 1128 for the spillback-throttle flag prototype.
- Ping infra to get a bare-metal node with NVLink disabled (for deterministic PCIe-only tests) and a node with NIC RDMA noise injection capability.

Rough TL;DR for folks skimming: PCIe-only interconnects produce higher variance and bursts in cross-GPU KV fetch latency, which leads to higher eviction churn and much worse tail latency. Short-term mitigations: throttle remote fetch concurrency, score eviction with cross-node cost, and prefer NVLink peers for spillback. Longer-term: topology-aware policies and batching/coalescing of cross-node fetches.
